Issued at 1023 AM MDT Sat Sep 12 2026

ISOLATED TO SCATTERED STORMS THIS WEEKEND: 

Modest moisture has begun to settle over the region this morning, 
prompting the sparse, weak showers and thunderstorms over Colorado's 
Western Slope. You may have also noticed a breezy morning thanks to 
decent mixing under the strong zonal flow, paired with a modest 
pressure gradient. These breezy conditions will continue to be 
around this afternoon as decent mixing continues to be favored. Also 
worth mentioning is shower activity will also contribute to windy 
conditions should gusty outflow winds develop. Shower and storm 
chances this afternoon will be relatively isolated in nature and so 
should impacts. By Sunday, storm coverage becomes more scattered as 
the next strong push of moisture begins to move in. PWATs begin to 
climb Sunday, with values upwards of 200% of normal, with the likely 
chance of exceeding the 75th percentile and approaching, if not 
surpassing the max values for mid September. 


COOLER AND WETTER PATTERN MONDAY AND BEYOND: 

By Monday, a deep trough begins to push into the PacNW. Due to 
cyclonic flow around a low, southwesterly flow will be favored over 
the southwestern CONUS. This means subtropical moisture will be 
pushed further inland, centering the strong plume of moisture over 
our CWA. PWATs continue to be forecasted over the 75th percentile 
for this time of year, which will be enough to prompt our next 
chance for widespread showers and storms.

Cloud cover is expected to be generally widespread come Monday, 
especially in the mornings. This has the ability to dictate storm 
potential each afternoon, which just might be enough to push storm 
mode in the stratiform direction. However, it is worth considering 
the dynamic forcing at play during this time period as well. 
Firstly, Sunday night into Monday will see a cold frontal passage 
which will include pockets of frontogenesis. Secondly, by Monday we 
are expected to be under the right entrance region of an upper level 
jet. This promotes areas of upper level divergence and surface level 
convergence. Both of these factors will go towards supporting 
discrete storm development (embedded stronger storms in stratiform 
rainfall). Whether these storms are isolated or widespread in 
nature, localized heavy rainfall is a possibility. Impacts from this 
rainfall will be enhanced in places that experienced multiple 
rounds of showers and storms the past weekend. 

In terms of QPF, the NBM continues to favor the southwestern facing 
slopes, particularly along the San Juans, Grand Mesa, and West Elks. 
Playing around with probabilities for those southwestern slopes 
shows a 60-80% chance of exceeding 0.75" of rain at least for the 
Grand Mesa and San Juans. As for the northeastern slopes, lower 
rainfall totals are likely, but still indicating some spots to see 
0.25" of rain. Although, if rain stratiforms out, these totals will 
likely decrease. It is important to note that there is still time 
for these factors to evolve before we can speculate on the likeliest 
scenario. Stay tuned for future updates, especially once more HiRes 
guidance becomes available. 

Look for daytime highs to cool down Monday and beyond due to that 
aforementioned frontal passage. For the rest of the work week, 
active weather will continue to be present. The moisture pool will 
continue to lock in over the Western Slope, with the upper level jet 
continuing to stretch across the Intermountain West. But, without 
clear signs of additional forcing, impacts from this moisture could 
be even more conditional on morning cloud cover. At this time, this 
is not a factor we can get too in the weeds about. By Friday, models 
are in agreement we see a dissipation of moisture, but not a 
complete elimination as PWATs still appear to be above normal.
